  format(get(a) - get(b), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)
}

}

p2521_coxph_results <- readr::read_tsv("data/public/p2521_coxph.tsv")

#wgs_phs <- readr::read_tsv("data/public/p212_wgs_phs_performance.tsv")

  filter(model == "any_pca", age == 70)

wgs_cuminc <- readr::read_tsv("data/public/p212_wgs_cuminc_at_age.tsv", show_col_types = FALSE)
# Percent decline per year in the PHS HR from the time-varying model: 100 * (1 - HR of tt(phs))
tt_decline <- function(coxph_results) {
  sprintf("%.1f", 100 * (1 - coxph_results$estimate[coxph_results$term == "tt(phs)"]))
}
# "est% (95% CI [lo, hi])" for a cumulative incidence stratum
ci_pct <- function(stratum) {
  r <- p2521_cuminc[p2521_cuminc$stratum == stratum, ]
  sprintf("%.1f%% (95%% CI [%.1f, %.1f])", 100 * r$estimate, 100 * r$conf_low, 100 * r$conf_high)
}
# "est (95% CI [lo, hi])" for the HUSK HR per SD in an age band
age_hr <- function(band) {
  r <- p2521_age_hr[p2521_age_hr$age_band == band, ]
  sprintf("%.2f, 95%% CI [%.2f, %.2f]", r$estimate, r$conf.low, r$conf.high)
}
# Share of all WGS-subset cases that fall in a group, as a rounded percent
wgs_case_share <- function(groups) {
  ev <- wgs_cuminc$events[wgs_cuminc$group %in% groups]
  round(100 * sum(ev) / sum(wgs_cuminc$events[wgs_cuminc$group %in% c("HOXB13 carrier", "HOXB13 non-carrier")]))
}

# Abstract {.unnumbered}

Background: Accurate risk prediction is needed to identify men at greatest risk of prostate cancer (PCa) while avoiding overdiagnosis of indolent disease. Polygenic hazard scores (PHS) are being tested for this purpose in prospective clinical screening trials.


Methods: We assessed the latest PHS model (PHS601) for predicting PCa and aggressive PCa in two Norwegian cohorts (N = `{r} format(p2521_sample_size[[1, 2]], big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)` and N = `{r} format(p212_sample_size[[1, 2]], big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)`). In a whole-genome sequencing (WGS) subset (N = `{r} format(wgs_summary[[1, 2]], big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)`), we compared PHS601 with rare pathogenic variants (RPVs) as pre-diagnosis screening tools. 

Results: PHS601 stratified risk of PCa (HR~80/20~ = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", p2521 |> filter(metric == "HR[80-100]_[0-20]") |> pull(estimate))`, 95\% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", p2521 |> filter(metric == "HR[80-100]_[0-20]") |> pull(conf_low))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", p2521 |> filter(metric == "HR[80-100]_[0-20]") |> pull(conf_high))`\]) and aggressive PCa (HR~80/20~ = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", p2521_meta |> filter(metric == "HR[80-100]_[0-20]") |> pull(estimate))`, 95% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", p2521_meta |> filter(metric == "HR[80-100]_[0-20]") |> pull(conf_low))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", p2521_meta |> filter(metric == "HR[80-100]_[0-20]") |> pull(conf_high))`\]). By age 70, estimated cumulative incidence was `{r} ci_pct("80-100%")` in the top PHS quintile versus `{r} ci_pct("0-20%")` in the bottom quintile. The PHS effect declined with age (HR per SD = `{r} age_hr("40-59")` at ages 40-59 vs `{r} age_hr("70+")` at ages 70 or older). HOXB13 pathogenic variants conferred high risk (`{r} wgs_cuminc$events[wgs_cuminc$group == "HOXB13 carrier"]`/`{r} wgs_cuminc$n[wgs_cuminc$group == "HOXB13 carrier"]` carriers diagnosed) but accounted for only `{r} wgs_case_share("HOXB13 carrier")`% of cases, whereas the top PHS quintile accounted for `{r} wgs_case_share("PHS 80-100%")`% in this WGS subset.

Conclusions: This first external validation of PHS601 in independent Norwegian population-based cohorts shows that PHS identifies far more high-risk men than known RPVs, with the strongest stratification at younger ages.

Impact: Genotype-based PHS could be used to start screening earlier in high-risk men and to defer it in low-risk men. These findings support prospective trials of PHS-guided screening.

# Introduction

Prostate cancer (PCa) is the second most commonly diagnosed cancer among men worldwide and a leading cause of cancer-related mortality [@bray2024]. Although early detection can reduce deaths from PCa, population screening with prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is limited by false positives, overdiagnosis, and overtreatment, particularly of indolent disease [@ilic2013; @roobol2025]. Therefore, there is a clinical need to identify men at elevated risk of early-onset PCa to focus early screening and downstream diagnostics (e.g., MRI), while minimizing harms.

PCa is highly heritable (~42%) [@lichtenstein2000] with risk influenced by rare pathogenic variants (RPVs) as well as common variants. RPVs, such as in BRCA1, BRCA2, and HOXB13, confer large increases in risk, but occur at low frequencies in the general population [@seibert2023]. Common variants typically have smaller effect sizes, but can be combined in polygenic models to estimate inherited risk. Furthermore, polygenic hazard scores (PHS) use time-to-event modeling, which allows for prediction of age at diagnosis [@desikan2017; @seibert2018; @huynh-le2021]. The latest age-of-onset PHS, PHS601, has been integrated with family history and genetic ancestry to form P-CARE (Prostate CAncer integrated Risk Evaluation) [@vassy2026], which is being implemented in a clinical trial of precision prostate cancer screening in the United States Department of Veterans Affairs healthcare system (Clinicaltrials.gov NCT05926102, registered July 3rd, 2023).

PHS601 was developed in the US Million Veterans Program, a large, multi-ethnic cohort, and showed robust replication in the PRACTICAL consortium, but independent validation in population-based cohorts is lacking [@vassy2026]. In addition, direct within-cohort comparisons of PHS-based stratification versus WGS-based RPV screening are limited. Here, we performed external validation of PHS601 in two Norwegian cohorts: a population study (Hordaland Health Studies; HUSK) and a clinical cohort enriched for family history of cancer (Norwegian Familial Cancer Study; NFCS). We evaluated whether PHS601 stratifies risk of PCa and aggressive PCa. We also leveraged whole-genome sequencing to compare PHS-based risk stratification with RPV carrier status. Our aim was to establish the performance of PHS601 for age-specific risk prediction in independent populations and to evaluate the relative utility of PHS versus RPV screening for genomically-informed cancer screening.

# Results

## PHS601 stratified PCa risk in two Norwegian cohorts

Participants with higher genetic risk scores in PHS601 showed greater risk of early diagnosis in both Norwegian cohorts. In the HUSK cohort (`{r} p2521_sample_size[1, 3]` cases and  `{r} format(p2521_sample_size[[1, 4]], big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)` controls), each SD increase in PHS was associated with an `r (round(p2521 |> filter(metric == "HR_SD") |> pull(estimate), 2) * 100) - 100`\% greater risk of PCa (HR~SD~ = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521 |> filter(metric == "HR_SD") |> pull(estimate), 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", p2521 |> filter(metric == "HR_SD") |> pull(conf_low))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", p2521 |> filter(metric == "HR_SD") |> pull(conf_high))`]), with individuals in the top quintile having over `{r} p2521 |> filter(metric == "HR[80-100]_[0-20]") |> pull(estimate) |> floor()` times the risk of those in the bottom quintile (HR~80/20~ = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", p2521 |> filter(metric == "HR[80-100]_[0-20]") |> pull(estimate))`, 95\% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", p2521 |> filter(metric == "HR[80-100]_[0-20]") |> pull(conf_low))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", p2521 |> filter(metric == "HR[80-100]_[0-20]") |> pull(conf_high))`\]; @{tbl-coxph} and @{fig-phs}). Results were similar in the NFCS cohort (`{r} p212_sample_size[1, 3]` cases and `{r} p212_sample_size[1, 4]` controls), where each SD increase in PHS conferred a twofold greater risk (HR~SD~ = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212 |> filter(metric == "HR_SD") |> pull(estimate), 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", p212 |> filter(metric == "HR_SD") |> pull(conf_low))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", p212 |> filter(metric == "HR_SD") |> pull(conf_high))`]; @{tbl-coxph}), with HR~80/20~ = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", p212 |> filter(metric == "HR[80-100]_[0-20]") |> pull(estimate))` (95\% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", p212 |> filter(metric == "HR[80-100]_[0-20]") |> pull(conf_low))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", p212 |> filter(metric == "HR[80-100]_[0-20]") |> pull(conf_high))`\]; @{tbl-coxph} and @{fig-phs}). Cumulative incidence in the HUSK cohort was generally consistent with national Cancer Registry data, with a notable lower rate of case ascertainment between age 50 and 70. However, the NFCS cohort showed substantially elevated baseline incidence relative to national data (Figure S1).

PHS effects were strongest at younger ages in both cohorts. Schoenfeld residuals tests revealed a negative trend in HR with age (HUSK: $\chi^2$ = `r round(p2521_zph[1, "chisq"], 2)`, p = `r pvalr(p2521_zph[1, "p"])`; NFCS: $\chi^2$ = `r round(p212_zph[1, "chisq"], 2)`, p = `r pvalr(p212_zph[1, "p"])`; Figure S2) confirmed with a time-varying Cox model with a linear age interaction, which showed that genetic risk declined by `{r} tt_decline(p2521_coxph_results)`-`{r} tt_decline(p212_coxph_results)`% per year (Table S4). Age-specific hazard ratios for the 40-59, 60-69 and 70+ age bands are shown in @tbl-age-hr.

Internal calibration was assessed across PHS quintiles at ages 50, 55, 60, and 65 years (Figure S3). For the age-varying PHS model, calibration slopes were close to unity at ages 55–65 in both cohorts; estimates were less precise at age 50, particularly in HUSK, due to low incidence rate. In HUSK, observed cumulative incidence in the highest PHS quintile at age 60 was approximately 4–5%, comparable to that in the median quintile at age 65. In NFCS, observed cumulative incidence in the highest quintile at age 55 was approximately 9%, compared with approximately 7–8% in the median quintile at age 65.

Adjusting for genetic PCs or excluding second- and third-degree relatives had little effect on the PHS associations, apart from reduced precision (Table S2).

## PHS601 was associated with aggressive PCa in Norwegian cohorts

In the HUSK cohort (`{r} p2521_sample_size[2, 3]` aggressive cases and `{r} format(p2521_sample_size[[2, 4]], big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)` controls), each SD increase in PHS was associated with a `{r} (round(p2521_meta |> filter(metric == "HR_SD") |> pull(estimate), 2) * 100) - 100`\% greater risk of aggressive disease (HR~SD~ = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_meta |> filter(metric == "HR_SD") |> pull(estimate), 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", p2521_meta |> filter(metric == "HR_SD") |> pull(conf_low))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", p2521_meta |> filter(metric == "HR_SD") |> pull(conf_high))`]), while individuals in the top quintile of PHS had `{r} p2521_meta |> filter(metric == "HR[80-100]_[0-20]") |> pull(estimate) |> floor()`-fold the risk of those in the bottom quintile (HR~80/20~ = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", p2521_meta |> filter(metric == "HR[80-100]_[0-20]") |> pull(estimate))`, 95% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", p2521_meta |> filter(metric == "HR[80-100]_[0-20]") |> pull(conf_low))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", p2521_meta |> filter(metric == "HR[80-100]_[0-20]") |> pull(conf_high))`\]; @{tbl-coxph} and @{fig-phs}). Similarly, in the NFCS cohort (`{r} p212_sample_size[2, 3]` aggressive cases and `{r} format(p212_sample_size[[2, 4]], big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)` controls), each SD increase in PHS conferred a `{r} (round(p212_meta |> filter(metric == "HR_SD") |> pull(estimate), 2) * 100) - 100`\% greater risk of aggressive disease (HR~SD~ = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_meta |> filter(metric == "HR_SD") |> pull(estimate), 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", p212_meta |> filter(metric == "HR_SD") |> pull(conf_low))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", p212_meta |> filter(metric == "HR_SD") |> pull(conf_high))`]), with HR~80/20~ = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", p212_meta |> filter(metric == "HR[80-100]_[0-20]") |> pull(estimate))` (95% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", p212_meta |> filter(metric == "HR[80-100]_[0-20]") |> pull(conf_low))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", p212_meta |> filter(metric == "HR[80-100]_[0-20]") |> pull(conf_high))`\]; @{tbl-coxph} and @{fig-phs}). However, it should be noted that the sample size of aggressive cases in the NFCS cohort was small (n = 46) resulting in wide confidence bands. Proportional hazards assumptions were not violated in either cohort based on statistical tests and weighted residual plots (HUSK: $\chi^2$ = `r round(p2521_zph[2, "chisq"], 2)`, p = `r pvalr(p2521_zph[2, "p"])`; NFCS: $\chi^2$ = `r round(p212_zph[2, "chisq"], 2)`, p = `r pvalr(p212_zph[2, "p"])`; Figure S2).

## PHS captures more high-risk men than than RPV screening across known PCa predisposition genes

We compared RPVs and PHS in predicting PCa risk in the NFCS cohort. Analyses were restricted to `{r} wgs_summary$wgs_1` participants with both WGS and genotyping (`{r} wgs_summary$status_1` cases and `{r} wgs_summary$wgs_1 - wgs_summary$status_1` controls) of whom `{r} wgs_summary$any_carrier_1` carried a predisposing mutation in one of the twelve target genes. Of the twelve potentially predisposing genes, only HOXB13 had an enrichment in the number of pathogenic variants among PCa cases compared to controls (OR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", fisher |> filter(gene == "HOXB13_carrier") |> pull(estimate))`, 95% LCB = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", fisher |> filter(gene == "HOXB13_carrier") |> pull(conf.low))`, adj. p = `{r} fisher |> filter(gene == "HOXB13_carrier") |> pull(p.adjust) |> pvalr(digits = 2)`; Table S5); subsequent survival models therefore focus on HOXB13 as the only gene with evidence of enrichment. 

In the WGS subset, a one-SD increase in PHS predicted a `{r} (wgs_results |> filter(model == "phs_wgs") |> pull(estimate) |> round(2) * 100) - 100`\% higher risk of PCa (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", wgs_results |> filter(model == "phs_wgs") |> pull(estimate))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", wgs_results |> filter(model == "phs_wgs") |> pull(conf.low))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", wgs_results |> filter(model == "phs_wgs") |> pull(conf.high))`], p `{r} wgs_results |> filter(model == "phs_wgs") |> pull(p.value) |> pvalr()`; @{fig-hoxb13}), while HOXB13 carriers had a `{r} wgs_results |> filter(model == "hoxb13_wgs") |> pull(estimate) |> round(1)`-fold greater risk than non-carriers (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", wgs_results |> filter(model == "hoxb13_wgs") |> pull(estimate))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", wgs_results |> filter(model == "hoxb13_wgs") |> pull(conf.low))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", wgs_results |> filter(model == "hoxb13_wgs") |> pull(conf.high))`], p `{r} wgs_results |> filter(model == "hoxb13_wgs") |> pull(p.value) |> pvalr()`). HOXB13 pathogenic variants occurred in `r round(wgs_summary$HOXB13_carrier_1 / wgs_summary$wgs_1 * 100, 1)`\% of participants. To enable direct comparison with this risk stratum, we evaluated individuals in the top `r round(wgs_summary$HOXB13_carrier_1 / wgs_summary$wgs_1 * 100, 1)`\% of the PHS distribution against the median. This high-risk PHS stratum demonstrated `{r} round(wgs_phs_95 |> filter(metric == "HR[98-100]_[30-70]") |> pull(estimate), 1)`-fold higher risk (HR~98.2/50~ = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_phs_95 |> filter(metric == "HR[98-100]_[30-70]") |> pull(estimate), 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_phs_95 |> filter(metric == "HR[98-100]_[30-70]") |> pull(conf_low), 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_phs_95 |> filter(metric == "HR[98-100]_[30-70]") |> pull(conf_high), 2))`]), compared with the HOXB13 HR above. HOXB13 carriers accounted for `{r} wgs_case_share("HOXB13 carrier")`% of cases (`{r} wgs_cuminc$events[wgs_cuminc$group == "HOXB13 carrier"]`/`{r} wgs_cuminc$n[wgs_cuminc$group == "HOXB13 carrier"]` carriers were diagnosed), whereas the top PHS quintile accounted for `{r} wgs_case_share("PHS 80-100%")`% of cases (Table S6).

# Discussion

We provide the first external validation of PHS601 in independent European population-based cohorts, demonstrating that the time-to-event genetic risk stratification of PHS601 generalizes across healthcare systems and populations with different baseline risk profiles, screening practices, and genetic backgrounds. The magnitude of risk stratification in HUSK (HR~80/20~ = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", p2521 |> filter(metric == "HR[80-100]_[0-20]") |> pull(estimate))`, 95\% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", p2521 |> filter(metric == "HR[80-100]_[0-20]") |> pull(conf_low))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", p2521 |> filter(metric == "HR[80-100]_[0-20]") |> pull(conf_high))`\]) was consistent with PHS601 replication in the PRACTICAL consortium (COSM: HR~80/20~ = 9.18, 95% CI \[6.66–12.93\]; ProtecT: HR~80/20~ = 5.67, 95% CI \[4.75, 6.73\])[@vassy2026]. To illustrate the clinical magnitude of this risk stratification: by age 70, men in the top PHS quintile had an estimated cumulative PCa incidence of `{r} ci_pct("80-100%")`, compared with `{r} ci_pct("0-20%")` for those in the bottom quintile (@{tbl-coxph}), a ~`{r} round(p2521_cuminc$estimate[p2521_cuminc$stratum == "80-100%"] / p2521_cuminc$estimate[p2521_cuminc$stratum == "0-20%"])`-fold absolute risk difference.

PHS601 stratified absolute risk of aggressive PCa at a similar magnitude to any-stage PCa, despite being trained on any-stage disease, which supports prior testing of PHS601 [@dornisch2025; @vassy2026] (HUSK: HR~80/20~ for aggressive = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", p2521_meta |> filter(metric == "HR[80-100]_[0-20]") |> pull(estimate))`, 95% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", p2521_meta |> filter(metric == "HR[80-100]_[0-20]") |> pull(conf_low))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", p2521_meta |> filter(metric == "HR[80-100]_[0-20]") |> pull(conf_high))`\] versus any-stage PCa = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", p2521 |> filter(metric == "HR[80-100]_[0-20]") |> pull(estimate))`, 95\% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", p2521 |> filter(metric == "HR[80-100]_[0-20]") |> pull(conf_low))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", p2521 |> filter(metric == "HR[80-100]_[0-20]") |> pull(conf_high))`\]). We assessed risk in the general population from birth, the appropriate framing for pre-screening, because a case-only analysis would condition on prior diagnosis [@paternoster2017]. 

The intended clinical use of PHS is to be an adjunct to age for choosing when to start and how often to screen for prostate cancer. High-PHS men may benefit from earlier and more intensive surveillance, while low-PHS men are candidates for reduced or deferred screening. The observed differences in cumulative incidence illustrate the potential clinical relevance of incorporating inherited risk alongside age: men in the highest PHS quintile reached cumulative incidence levels comparable to those of men in the median quintile approximately five years earlier in HUSK and ten years earlier in NFCS (Figure S3). These findings support further evaluation of PHS-guided screening strategies in which men with high inherited risk could be considered for earlier screening.

In addition to testing the performance of PHS, we tested twelve known PCa predisposition genes and found that, in this dataset, genotyping-based PHS provided stronger population-level risk stratification than WGS-based RPV screening. Among the RPVs we tested, only HOXB13 showed enrichment in cases, and while HOXB13 carriers have a very high risk, with `{r} wgs_cuminc$events[wgs_cuminc$group == "HOXB13 carrier"]`/`{r} wgs_cuminc$n[wgs_cuminc$group == "HOXB13 carrier"]` carriers receiving a diagnosis, it only accounted for `{r} wgs_case_share("HOXB13 carrier")`% of cases, whereas the top PHS quintile accounted for `{r} wgs_case_share("PHS 80-100%")`% of cases (`{r} sprintf("%.1f", 100 * wgs_cuminc$estimate[wgs_cuminc$group == "PHS 80-100%"])`% cumulative incidence by age 70, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.1f", 100 * wgs_cuminc$conf_low[wgs_cuminc$group == "PHS 80-100%"])`, `{r} sprintf("%.1f", 100 * wgs_cuminc$conf_high[wgs_cuminc$group == "PHS 80-100%"])`]; Table S6). Therefore, a much larger percentage of the population is affected by a high risk score than is affected by currently known RPVs [@seibert2023], which means genetic risk scoring may be more useful for screening at the population level. Notably, genotyping with imputation successfully identified all HOXB13 carriers subsequently confirmed by WGS, suggesting that for population-scale PCa screening, a single genotyping array can simultaneously generate PHS and capture the only known high-effect PCa variant evaluated here.

Though PHS captures more at-risk men than HOXB13 in the pre-screening context, RPVs provide additional value in other clinical applications. For example, individuals with BRCA mutations may benefit from PARP inhibitors [@turk2018], and RPVs have different implications for genetic counseling, particularly regarding risk to offspring. There remains value in screening for RPVs in appropriate clinical contexts. 

We observed a weak but significant negative trend in the HR of PHS with age in two independent cohorts such that the strongest effect of genetic risk was at the youngest ages (Figure S2). In time-varying models, this corresponded to an estimated decline in genetic effect size of approximately `{r} tt_decline(p2521_coxph_results)`-`{r} tt_decline(p212_coxph_results)`% per year (Table S4). This age-dependent attenuation of genetic risk is consistent with observations from other complex diseases and may reflect several biological processes. Accumulating environmental exposures, somatic mutations, and stochastic processes may increasingly dominate over germline variation with age [@jiang2021; @winkler2024], and competing mortality may leave a selected survivor population at older ages. Stronger genetic effects at younger ages have also been documented for BRCA1/2 in breast cancer [@kuchenbaecker2017]. These findings identify the age range where genetic risk stratification may be most actionable for prevention and early detection.

This study has several limitations. We did not have access to family history data or PSA measurements for all participants. While family history provides additional information beyond PHS601 at the population level, and is included as an independent predictor in the integrated P-CARE model [@vassy2026], future work should explore integration of PHS with other clinical risk factors and with social determinants of health, lifestyle factors, and environmental exposures [@plym2023; @pagadala2024; @pagadala2024a]. The NFCS cohort was enriched for family history of cancer and is not representative of the general Norwegian population (Figure S1); absolute risk estimates were therefore derived from the population-based HUSK cohort. HR estimates come from cohorts recruited much earlier than the 2014-2017 registry incidence in @{fig-strat}; because PSA testing and MRI use have changed substantially (Figure S1), the projected absolute risks in @{fig-strat} are model-based estimates rather than direct contemporary screening risks. Whole-genome sequencing was available only in a subset of NFCS, which reduced power for very rare variant analyses and does not preclude additional rarer variants with larger effects; therefore, the PHS-versus-RPV comparison should be interpreted as a comparison of observed effect sizes in this dataset. Future implementation studies should also evaluate performance and assess equity across diverse ancestry and healthcare groups to avoid widening disparities. The strong risk stratification observed here provides a foundation for prospective trials of risk-stratified screening in Norway, but cost-effectiveness analyses will be needed before clinical implementation to identify optimal screening thresholds and age ranges.

PHS601 provides strong risk stratification for prostate cancer and aggressive disease in independent Norwegian population-based cohorts, and identifies far more high-risk men than known rare pathogenic variants. Its effect is strongest at younger ages, when risk-adapted screening could start earlier for high-PHS men and be deferred for low-PHS men. These findings support prospective trials of PHS-guided precision screening for PCa.


# Materials and Methods

## Study Population

This study evaluated two Norwegian cohorts (@tbl-age-summary). The first cohort was the Hordaland Health Studies (Helseundersøkelsene i Hordaland; HUSK) with `{r} cn("p2521", "source_cohort")` participants. This cohort was recruited from Hordaland county in western Norway in two waves. The first wave was in 1992-1993 and the second wave was in 1997-1999. Analyses were restricted to the `{r} cn("p2521", "source_males")` male participants in HUSK. The second cohort was the Norwegian Familial Cancer Study (NFCS) with `{r} cn("p212", "source_cohort")` participants [@mattingsdal2021]. Participants in this cohort were recruited in 1980-1995 from all of Norway via self-report based on over-representation of cancer in their families. Analyses were restricted to the `{r} cn("p212", "source_males")` male participants in NFCS. End of follow-up was defined by the last recorded clinical contact in linked registry data. The latest delivery was 2025 for HUSK and 2020 for NFCS.

Within the male participants, the analysis set was restricted to those with genotype data passing QC, a PHS, complete age and PCa status data, and age 40 years or older (HUSK n = `{r} cn("p2521", "male_with_phs_and_complete_phenotype_age40plus")`; NFCS n = `{r} cn("p212", "male_with_phs_and_complete_phenotype_age40plus")`). Participants last observed before age 40 were excluded because diagnoses before this age were unavailable; age 40 was the time origin in the time-varying models. After removing duplicates and monozygotic twins (see Relatedness), the primary analysis sets comprised `{r} cn("p2521", "age40plus_after_king_0deg")` HUSK and `{r} cn("p212", "age40plus_after_king_0deg")` NFCS participants (@tbl-age-summary).

## Ethics approval

The study protocol was approved by the Norwegian Regional Ethics Committee (REK) Sør-Øst, IDs 2015/2382 (NFCS cohort) and 270326 (HUSK cohort).

## Characterization of PCa Cases

In both cohorts, PCa cases were defined as participants with ICD10 code C61. Diagnosis date was the first instance of this ICD10 code in the Cancer Registry of Norway, which has been estimated to be 98.8% complete [@larsen2009]. Age was used as the time scale, with follow-up from birth to age at diagnosis (event) or age at last follow-up (censoring). Deaths prior to prostate cancer diagnosis were treated as censoring events. Aggressive disease was defined according to metastasis codes `{r} metastase_strict[1:length(metastase_strict)-1]`, and `{r} metastase_strict[length(metastase_strict)]` in the Norwegian Cancer Registry, corresponding to disease that extends to lymph nodes inside or outside the same body region, organ metastasis outside the body region, and microscopic or macroscopic ingrowth into neighboring structures (Table S1). For the HUSK and NFCS cohorts, 84% and 98% of aggressive cases were captured at diagnosis, while the remaining cases had a median follow-up time from initial PCa diagnosis to aggressive diagnosis of 10 days, so we treat aggressive PCa as captured at initial diagnosis.

## Genotyping and PHS calculation

### Genotyping

HUSK participants were genotyped at deCODE Genetics (https://www.decode.com/) in two batches (10,083 and 25,432 individuals in batch 1 and 2, respectively) using a customized Illumina GSA v3 array (687,316 genotyped variants). Genotyping data were QCed separately for each batch using plink2 [@purcell2007], removing indels, non-ATGC, strand-ambiguous, poorly-genotyped (--geno 0.05), non-autosomal and rare (--maf 0.05) variants, variants with extreme deviation from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (--hwe 1E-50 midp keep-fewhet), and variants that could not be aligned to the HGDP + 1KG reference panel from gnomAD [@koenig2024] or whose MAF deviated from it by more than 30%. After merging the batches, variants with high missingness (--geno 0.02) and individuals with poor genotyping rate (--mind 0.05) were removed. The combined dataset was then phased and imputed with Beagle 5.4 (version 27May24.118) using the HGDP + 1KG reference panel. The resulting dataset contained 10,433,751 autosomal variants.

For the NFCS cohort, participants were genotyped from peripheral blood DNA using the Illumina OmniExpress 24 v1.1 chip at deCODE genetics. The genotyped dataset consisted of 713,014 SNPs. Genotype data were imputed using the HRC v1.1 reference panel following the same imputation protocol as The Norwegian Mother, Father and Child Cohort [@corfield2024]. After imputation, the dataset consisted of 39,111,193 autosomal variants.

We assessed genetic relatedness using KING [@manichaikul2010]. The primary analyses used the 0-degree retained set (kinship cutoff 0.35), retaining one participant per duplicate- or monozygotic-twin-level pair. This removed `{r} cn("p2521", "age40plus_removed_by_king_0deg")` participants from the HUSK analysis set and `{r} cn("p212", "age40plus_removed_by_king_0deg")` from the NFCS analysis set, leaving the primary analysis samples described above. Sensitivity analyses used retained sets with kinship cutoffs of 0.088 (second-degree or closer; HUSK n = `{r} cn("p2521", "age40plus_after_king_2deg")`, NFCS n = `{r} cn("p212", "age40plus_after_king_2deg")`) and 0.044 (third-degree or closer; HUSK n = `{r} cn("p2521", "age40plus_after_king_3deg")`, NFCS n = `{r} cn("p212", "age40plus_after_king_3deg")`). Sample sizes and events for each retained set are reported in Table S2. Genetic principal components were calculated using FlashPCA on LD-pruned autosomal variants after excluding high-LD regions [@abraham2017]. At each relatedness threshold, models were fitted without PC adjustment and with adjustment for the first five or ten PCs.

### Harmonization of alleles and calculation of PHS

The list of variants used by the PHS601 model, and their effect sizes, were acquired by contacting the authors [@vassy2026]. Chromosome X imputation was not available in our genotype data so the 21 SNPs in the original model on chromosome X were removed leaving 580 SNPs. Imputed genotype data in each cohort and model variants were matched by genomic position and alleles, resulting in 485 variants (in HUSK) and 557 variants (in NFCS) used for PHS computation. Strand-ambiguous variants were retained, after verifying that no strand flips were present among non-strand ambiguous SNPs in either of the two cohorts. Polygenic hazard scores were calculated for each cohort using `plink --score` [@purcell2007]. Missing genotypes contributed an amount proportional to the imputed allele frequency.

## Whole-genome sequencing

### Sequencing

This retrospective analysis used previously generated WGS data from 2,576 participants of the NFCS cohort, as described previously [@ivarsdottir2024]. The WGS subset was selected to represent a range of cancer diagnoses across both sexes, and thus was deliberately enriched for cancer cases, but not specifically for prostate cancer cases. This can be observed in the higher case rate and average PHS for this subset (@tbl-age-summary). The WGS data were generated at deCODE Genetics on Illumina HiSeqX and NovaSeq platforms. Only samples with genome-wide average coverage of at least 20× (mean 37.2X) were included, contaminated samples were removed using `read_haps` [@eggertsson2021], and joint variant calling was performed using GraphTyper (v.2.7.5) [@eggertsson2017]. Of the `{r} cn("p212", "wgs_flagged_source_cohort")` sequenced participants present in the NFCS phenotype data, `{r} cn("p212", "wgs_flagged_males")` were male. The WGS analyses used the `{r} cn("p212", "wgs_males_with_phs_and_complete_phenotype_age40plus")` of these with a PHS, complete phenotype data and age 40 years or older (`{r} cd("p212", "wgs_flagged_males", "wgs_males_with_phs_and_complete_phenotype")` lacked a PHS or complete phenotype data and `{r} cd("p212", "wgs_males_with_phs_and_complete_phenotype", "wgs_males_with_phs_and_complete_phenotype_age40plus")` were younger than 40). No kinship exclusion was applied to this subset.

### Variant calling and classification of RPVs

Identification of RPVs in the WGS dataset was performed using the Cancer Predisposition Sequencing Reporter – CPSR v2.2.0 [@nakken2021]. Specifically, we used CPSR to screen WGS variant calls for heterozygous and homozygous SNVs/InDels in high-penetrance prostate cancer genes, including BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, PALB2, CHEK2, HOXB13, MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, TP53, and EPCAM. Coding variants in these genes classified as pathogenic according to ClinVar (release 2025_03) were considered RPVs (Table S3). Of note, the HOXB13 G84E variant (rs138213197) was included in PHS601 and was also identified among the RPVs in whole-genome sequenced participants. All participants carrying the G84E mutation in WGS data also carried rs138213197 in the imputed genotype data.

## Statistical Analysis

### Polygenic hazard score performance evaluation

Polygenic hazard scores were evaluated in both cohorts using Cox proportional hazards models using the `coxph` function from the `survival` package in `R` [@survival-package]. Polygenic hazard scores were centered and scaled prior to model fit. Performance of each model is reported as HR~SD~, which is the increase in risk for a one-SD increase in PHS, HR~80/20~, which is the hazard ratio between the top 20% and the bottom 20% of PHS, and Harrell's concordance index (C-index). For these metrics, 95% confidence intervals were generated using `{r} bootstrap_iters` bootstrap iterations. All Cox models were evaluated for the proportional hazards assumption using `cox.zph` and by inspecting plots of the Schoenfeld residuals versus time [@grambsch1994]. For models that did not meet these assumptions, we performed sensitivity analysis with time-dependent covariates and a linear time transform (i.e., PHS $\cdot$ age) for the time-dependent PHS with the `tt` function. To report the age dependence directly, we also fitted a Cox model with a separate PHS coefficient in each of three age bands (40-59, 60-69 and 70 years or older; with follow-up split at ages 60 and 70) and tested heterogeneity across bands with a likelihood ratio test against a single constant HR.

### Rare pathogenic variant screening and comparison to polygenic risk

We assessed the effect of RPVs on PCa risk using WGS data from the whole-genome sequenced subset of the NFCS cohort. We first tested whether RPVs in any of the twelve genes were enriched among cases versus controls using a one-sided Fisher's exact test (one for each gene plus one for any-gene carrier status for a total of thirteen tests). Genes with significant enrichment (Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p < 0.05) were then modeled in Cox proportional hazards analyses to estimate HR between carriers and non-carriers and C-index. To compare the RPV risk stratum to PHS, we restricted analyses to participants with both WGS and genotyping data, refitting the PHS Cox model in this subset and calculating HR for a PHS percentile stratum matching the RPV carrier frequency.

### Comparison with Norwegian Cancer Registry data

To evaluate how generalizable our results were to the population of Norway, we compared the cumulative incidence in each cohort for both PCa (any stage) and for aggressive PCa to the cumulative incidence from the Cancer Registry of Norway (using the same ICD10 code and metastasis codes as before). We used annualized age-specific incidence rate binned by 5-year age groups for the years 2014-2017, as previously reported [@huynh-le2020a]. To convert these rates into cumulative incidence, we fit a log-quadratic (PCa) or log-linear (aggressive PCa) model to the 5-year group rates, predicted annualized incidence, and summed it over age. We compared these to the cumulative incidence derived from the Cox models in each cohort and stratified the cumulative incidence curves by HRs from the PHS Cox proportional hazards model fit to the HUSK data.

## Use of generative AI

GitHub Copilot, a generative AI tool, was used to assist with the analysis and visualization of data, including writing and revising the analysis code for the statistical analyses and figures described above. All AI-assisted code was reviewed by the authors and the resulting outputs were checked by the authors, who take full responsibility for the analyses and results reported. GitHub Copilot was also used to improve the writing of the manuscript, as described in the Acknowledgments.

## Data Availability

Data from the Norwegian Mother, Father and Child Cohort Study (MoBa) and the Medical Birth Registry of Norway are administered by the Norwegian Institute of Public Health and are not publicly available due to ethical and legal restrictions. Access may be granted to qualified researchers following approval from the Regional Committees for Medical and Health Research Ethics (REC), compliance with the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), and permission from the data owners. Participant consent does not allow for deposition of individual-level data in public repositories. Researchers seeking access for replication or further analyses must apply through the Norwegian health data access portal (helsedata.no) and enter a data access agreement with MoBa.

The data that support the findings of this study are not publicly available due to patient privacy and ethical restrictions. Data were accessed through the Tjenester for Sensitive Data facilities owned by the University of Oslo under ethics approval by the Regional Committee for Medical Research Ethics South East Norway. Inquiries about data access should be directed to the Regional Committees for Medical and Health Research Ethics of Norway.

Data from the Hordaland Health Studies (HUSK) are administered by the University of Bergen and data from the Norwegian Familial Cancer Study (NFCS) are not publicly available due to ethical and legal restrictions. Access may be granted to qualified researchers following approval from the Regional Committees for Medical and Health Research Ethics (REC), compliance with the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), and permission from the data owners.

## Code Availability

The scripts to recreate the analysis, figures, and manuscript can be accessed on GitHub at https://github.com/amorris28/heritable_cancer.

# Figure Legends {.unnumbered}

**Figure 1.** Cumulative incidence of PCa by age and stratified by centile ranges of PHS for the HUSK (A, C) and NFCS (B, D) cohorts. A and B show any-stage PCa and C and D show aggressive PCa. Time of event is age at diagnosis of PCa (A, B) or aggressive PCa (C, D). Controls were censored at age of last observation. Error ribbons are the 95% confidence interval. Please note the shrinking risk set after age 70, particularly in the 95-100% stratum, with corresponding reduced confidence in the prediction.

**Figure 2.** Cumulative incidence of PCa by age for the whole-genome sequenced subsample of the NFCS cohort stratified by either centile ranges of PHS or HOXB13 carrier status. Time of event is age at diagnosis of PCa (any stage). Controls were censored at age of last observation. Error ribbons are the 95% confidence interval. It should be noted that the HOXB13 carrier curve was based on a very small number of carriers (n = 9) as can be seen from the wide confidence intervals.

**Figure 3.** Predicted cumulative incidence of PCa and aggressive PCa in the general population of Norway based on data from the Norwegian Cancer Registry. The population baseline reflects PCa cases in Norway from 2014-2017 [@huynh-le2020a]. Curves were generated by calculating the HR for each stratum relative to the median (e.g., HR~95/50~) in the HUSK cohort and multiplying it by the baseline curve from the registry data. Confidence intervals were similarly derived based on the 95% boostrap CI for each stratum from 999 bootstrap iterations. The decline in incidence after age 70 observed for any-stage PCa is likely due to decreased screening rather than a true reduction in incidence.
